title: Asking for things: て-form and ください

grammarPoints.rule: The て-form is the shape everything else attaches to — requests now, whole chains of actions later. る-verbs make it by swapping る for て: たべる → たべて, みる → みて. On its own it is what you say to a friend: たべて = 'eat', 'go on, eat'.

antiPattern.ja: しゃしんを みるて。
antiPattern.why: る-verbs drop る before て — みる→みて, never みるて.

grammarPoints.rule: う-verbs change their last kana before て. The biggest row takes three endings at once: う・つ・る → って. かう→かって, たつ→たって, やる→やって. The kana before って never changes — only the ending does. Learn this table once and it pays twice: the past form た uses exactly the same rows.

antiPattern.why: う・つ・る drop their last kana before って — かう→かって, never かうて.

grammarPoints.rule: The second row is the voiced one: む・ぶ・ぬ → んで. のむ→のんで, あそぶ→あそんで. Notice it is んで, not んて — the ん drags the ending into a voiced で. (ぬ verbs are almost extinct in modern Japanese: しぬ 'to die' is essentially the only one, and it behaves exactly like のむ — しぬ→しんで. You will not need to produce it here.)

antiPattern.why: のむ ends in む, so it takes the んで row — のんで, never のみて.

grammarPoints.rule: Three rows are one kana each, and each one is different: く → いて (きく→きいて); ぐ → いで — the voiced twin of いて, just like んで was of んて (いそぐ→いそいで); す → して (かす→かして). Watch かう→かって against かす→かして: same first kana, different ending, different row. The ENDING decides, never the word.

antiPattern.why: く takes the いて row — きく→きいて, never きくて.

grammarPoints.rule: Three verbs ignore the table. する → して and くる → きて are the two irregulars you already know as a pair. The third is いく: it ends in く, so the table promises いいて — but it is いって, borrowing the う・つ・る row. Memorise these three as a set.

antiPattern.why: いく looks like a く-verb but skips the く→いて row — its て-form is いって.

grammarPoints.rule: て + ください = a polite request: 'please do X'. It is a fixed FORMULA — you attach ください to the て-form and nothing else changes. Drop ください and the bare て-form is the casual version friends use: みて = 'look', みてください = 'please look'.

antiPattern.why: ください attaches to the て-form, not the dictionary form — たべてください

grammarPoints.rule: A request needs something to request, and food is where a beginner starts. ごはん is cooked rice — and, by extension, the meal built round it. しょくじ is the meal itself, the sit-down occasion: しょくじを する is 'to have a meal'. たべもの is food in general, and ちゃ is tea. Whatever you eat, drink or ask for takes を. And to ask someone NOT to do something, you swap the て-form for the ない-form and add で: たべて → たべないで = 'don't eat it'. Same shape, opposite instruction — 「ミカの たべものを たべないで」 is 'don't eat Mika's food'.

で marks WHERE an action happens, and for a beginner that is the shop: みせで かう is 'buy it at the shop'. What you buy there is こめ — uncooked rice, the bag on the shelf, not the cooked bowl on the table (that one is ごはん). Getting to the shop is still に, not で: みせに いく.

antiPattern.why: に is where a thing IS; the place you do something takes で — いえで たべる.

grammarPoints.rule: ください is the polite half, and it detaches. みてください → みて: same verb, same て-form, and the whole difference in politeness lives in whether ください is there. Bare て for friends and family; keep ください for teachers, shopkeepers and people you have just met.
